Spatial model checking

Lecture 11. From the spatial logic SLCS to VoxLogicA 2.1.

Programming Languages Lab · University of Pisa
Vincenzo Ciancia, CNR-ISTI
vincenzo.ciancia@isti.cnr.it · github.com/vincenzoml/PLDW

Brain tumour delineation

In lecture 0 we saw this task: before radiotherapy, someone draws the tumour on the scan, slice by slice.

We also saw a short program that does it. This lecture explains that program: the logic its words come from, how a formula is computed on an image, and how the implementation has changed since 2019.

The program from lecture 0


let brain        = !touch(flair <. 0.1, border)
let pflair       = percentiles(flair, brain, 0.5)
let hyperIntense = flt(5.0, pflair >. 0.95)
let veryIntense  = flt(2.0, pflair >. 0.86)
let tumour       = grow(hyperIntense, veryIntense)

The brain is what does not touch the border of the image. The tumour is the brightest 5% of the brain, grown into the brightest 14% around it.

VoxLogicA, in G. Belmonte, V. Ciancia, D. Latella, M. Massink, TACAS 2019.

A logic and a model checker

A spatial logic is used as a description language. A model checker is its interpreter.

Together they give a declarative domain-specific language for graphs, images and 3D meshes.

  • A formula describes a property of points: "dark, and touching the border".
  • A model is a space, with facts about its points: an image and its colours.
  • The model checker computes the set of points where the formula holds: for an image, another image.

The same shape as evaluate(expression, environment) in lecture 4: a syntax, a semantic domain, and a function from one to the other.

One logic, several kinds of space

  • Reachability in a maze.
  • Annotation of maps.
  • GPS traces of moving vehicles.
  • Medical images, in 2D and 3D.

The formulas are the same in each case. What changes is the space: a graph, a grid of pixels, a grid of voxels.

A sentence we would like to evaluate

All the purple dogs will turn red, unless they are no more than 7 metres from the region where all the pink elephants will be tomorrow.

To give it a meaning we must decide a few things first.

spaceIs it discrete or continuous?
metricIs there a distance, so that "7 metres" means something?
factsWhat are the atomic facts: "purple", "dog"?
timeIs time involved, and how?

These are choices of a semantic domain. In this lecture the domain comes first, the syntax second, the interpreter third.

Plan of the lecture

  1. Modal logic read on topological spaces (1944).
  2. Closure spaces, and the spatial logic SLCS.
  3. Model checking: one algorithm per operator.
  4. VoxLogicA: the language and its interpreter.
  5. Medical imaging.
  6. VoxLogicA 2: logic and neural networks in one language.
  7. VoxLogicA 2.1: a new engine for the same language.
  8. An experiment that is still running.

Modal logic

\( \Phi ::= p \mid \neg \Phi \mid \Phi \wedge \Phi \mid \Diamond \Phi \)

A Kripke frame (Kripke, 1959) is a set of worlds \(W\) with a relation \(R\). A model adds which atomic propositions hold in which world.

\( x \models \Diamond\Phi \iff \exists y.\; x\,R\,y \wedge y \models \Phi \)

\(\Diamond\Phi\) is read "possibly \(\Phi\)". Its dual is \(\Box\Phi = \neg\Diamond\neg\Phi\), "necessarily \(\Phi\)".

The same syntax can be read on other structures. In 1944 McKinsey and Tarski read it on topological spaces.

S. A. Kripke. A Completeness Theorem in Modal Logic. Journal of Symbolic Logic 24(1), 1959.

Topological spaces

A topological space is a set \(X\) with a family of subsets called open: it contains \(\emptyset\) and \(X\), and it is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.

A set is closed when its complement is open.

A neighbourhood of a point \(x\) is a set that contains an open set containing \(x\). In the plane, every disc centred in \(x\) is one.

The closure \(\mathcal{C}(A)\) is the smallest closed set containing \(A\): \(A\) together with its boundary.

The interior \(\mathcal{I}(A)\) is defined as the dual of closure: the complement of the closure of the complement.

\( \mathcal{I}(A) = X \setminus \mathcal{C}(X \setminus A) \)

It is the largest open set contained in \(A\).

Kuratowski's closure axioms

A topology can be given by its closure operator alone. An operator \(\mathcal{C}\) on the subsets of \(X\) is the closure of a topology exactly when

\( \mathcal{C}(\emptyset) = \emptyset \)nothing is close to the empty set
\( A \subseteq \mathcal{C}(A) \)every point is close to itself
\( \mathcal{C}(A \cup B) = \mathcal{C}(A) \cup \mathcal{C}(B) \)closure goes through unions
\( \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{C}(A)) = \mathcal{C}(A) \)closing twice adds nothing

The closed sets are then the sets with \(\mathcal{C}(A) = A\).

Open sets and closure, side by side

Open sets \(\tau\)

  • \( \emptyset \in \tau,\ X \in \tau \)
  • \( U, V \in \tau \Rightarrow U \cap V \in \tau \)
  • \( U_i \in \tau \text{ for all } i \Rightarrow \bigcup_i U_i \in \tau \)

A set is closed when its complement is open.

Closure \(\mathcal{C}\)

  • \( \mathcal{C}(\emptyset) = \emptyset \)
  • \( A \subseteq \mathcal{C}(A) \)
  • \( \mathcal{C}(A \cup B) = \mathcal{C}(A) \cup \mathcal{C}(B) \)
  • \( \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{C}(A)) = \mathcal{C}(A) \)

Interior is its dual: \( \mathcal{I}(A) = X \setminus \mathcal{C}(X \setminus A) \).

\( \mathcal{C}(A) = \bigcap \{\, F \mid A \subseteq F,\ F \text{ closed} \,\} \)

\( F \text{ closed} \iff \mathcal{C}(F) = F \)

The two definitions give the same spaces. The one on the right is an operation on sets, and that is what the logic uses.

McKinsey and Tarski, 1944

Read \(\Diamond\) as closure and \(\Box\) as interior.

\( ⟦\Diamond\Phi⟧ = \mathcal{C}(⟦\Phi⟧) \qquad ⟦\Box\Phi⟧ = \mathcal{I}(⟦\Phi⟧) \)

  • A formula denotes a set of points: \(⟦p⟧\) is where \(p\) holds, \(⟦\neg\Phi⟧\) is the complement, \(⟦\Phi \wedge \Psi⟧\) the intersection.
  • \(\Diamond\Phi\) holds at the points that are close to \(\Phi\). \(\Box\Phi\) holds at the points well inside \(\Phi\).
  • Kuratowski's axioms, read as formulas, correspond to the axioms of the modal logic S4.

J. C. C. McKinsey, A. Tarski. The Algebra of Topology. Annals of Mathematics 45(1), 1944.

Closure and interior, in a picture

  • A point is in \(\mathcal{C}(A)\) when every neighbourhood of it meets \(A\), even a point on an edge that \(A\) does not contain.
  • A point is in \(\mathcal{I}(A)\) when some neighbourhood of it is contained in \(A\): no point of an edge is.

Solid edge: included. Dashed edge: excluded. \(A\) contains its top and left edges only. \(\mathcal{C}(A) \setminus \mathcal{I}(A)\) is the boundary.

Exercise: a lollipop

In the plane, red holds on an open disc (its circle excluded) and on a segment that touches the disc at one point.

Where do these hold?

  • \(\Box\,\)red
  • \(\Diamond\,\)red
  • \(\Diamond\,\)red \(\wedge \neg\Box\,\)red
  • \(\Diamond\Box\,\)red
  • red \(\wedge \neg\Diamond\Box\,\)red

Exercise: the answers

Dashed: the circle is excluded. A thin segment has no interior, so \(\Box\,\)red loses it. The last formula holds exactly on the segment, without the point where it touches the disc.

From topology to images

On a grid of pixels, the closure of a set adds the pixels one step away from it. Applied again, it adds the pixels two steps away: \(\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{C}(A)) \neq \mathcal{C}(A)\).

The last of Kuratowski's axioms fails, so a grid with this closure is not a topological space.

Čech closure spaces

Čech studied closure operators without the last axiom. A closure space is a set \(X\) with an operator \(\mathcal{C}\) such that

\( \mathcal{C}(\emptyset) = \emptyset \qquad A \subseteq \mathcal{C}(A) \qquad \mathcal{C}(A \cup B) = \mathcal{C}(A) \cup \mathcal{C}(B) \)

Topological spaces are the closure spaces where closure is idempotent. Interior is defined as before, as the dual of closure.

E. Čech. Topological Spaces. Wiley, 1966.

Closure from a relation

Every relation \(R\) on a set \(X\) gives a closure: a set, plus every point that one of its points is related to.

\( \mathcal{C}_R(A) = A \cup \{\, x \mid \exists a \in A.\; a \mathrel{R} x \,\} \)

These are the quasi-discrete closure spaces. Every graph is one, and the closure is not idempotent.

An image is a graph

The pixels are the points. Each pixel is related to the pixels around it.

In 2D, VoxLogicA relates a pixel to its 8 neighbours; in 3D, a voxel to its 26 neighbours.

The atomic facts are facts about one point: "its intensity is above 0.95", "it is blue".

What a model is

The syntax says which formulas can be written. A model says what they mean: it gives a structure, and says where each atomic proposition holds.

A Kripke model with four worlds. In orange, the atomic propositions true in each world. \(\Diamond q\) holds in \(w_1\) only: it is the only world with a successor where \(q\) holds.

Models, in formulas

Kripke model

\( \mathcal{M} = (W, R, \mathcal{V}) \qquad \mathcal{V} : AP \to 2^{W} \)

\( \mathcal{M}, w \models p \iff w \in \mathcal{V}(p) \)

\( \mathcal{M}, w \models \Diamond\Phi \iff \exists w'.\; w\,R\,w' \wedge \mathcal{M}, w' \models \Phi \)

Closure model

\( \mathcal{M} = (X, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{V}) \qquad \mathcal{V} : AP \to 2^{X} \)

\( \mathcal{M}, x \models p \iff x \in \mathcal{V}(p) \)

\( \mathcal{M}, x \models \mathcal{N}\Phi \iff x \in \mathcal{C}(⟦\Phi⟧) \)

\(AP\) is the set of atomic propositions, and \(\mathcal{V}\) is the valuation. In both cases the meaning of a formula is the set of points where it holds: \( ⟦\Phi⟧ = \{\, x \mid \mathcal{M}, x \models \Phi \,\} \).

A closure model

Each point is related to the points above, below, left and right of it. The atomic propositions are the colours. The next slides use this grid.

The Spatial Logic of Closure Spaces

\( \Phi ::= p \mid \top \mid \neg \Phi \mid \Phi \wedge \Phi \mid \mathcal{N}\,\Phi \mid \Phi\,\mathcal{S}\,\Psi \)

\( p,\ \top,\ \neg,\ \wedge \)an atomic proposition, true, negation, conjunction
\( \mathcal{N}\,\Phi \)near \(\Phi\): the closure of the points of \(\Phi\)
\( \Phi\,\mathcal{S}\,\Psi \)\(\Phi\) surrounded by \(\Psi\)

Disjunction, interior, boundary and reachability are derived from these.

V. Ciancia, D. Latella, M. Loreti, M. Massink. Model Checking Spatial Logics for Closure Spaces. Logical Methods in Computer Science 12(4), 2016.

Each formula denotes a set of points

\( ⟦p⟧ = \mathcal{V}(p) \)where the valuation says \(p\) holds
\( ⟦\top⟧ = X \)every point
\( ⟦\neg\Phi⟧ = X \setminus ⟦\Phi⟧ \)complement
\( ⟦\Phi \wedge \Psi⟧ = ⟦\Phi⟧ \cap ⟦\Psi⟧ \)intersection
\( ⟦\mathcal{N}\,\Phi⟧ = \mathcal{C}(⟦\Phi⟧) \)closure
\( ⟦\Phi\,\mathcal{S}\,\Psi⟧ \)defined with paths: next slides

Each case is one operation on sets, except the last.

Near

The ringed points satisfy \(\mathcal{N}\,\)red: the red points, and the points one step away from a red point.

Exercise: which red points satisfy \(\mathcal{N}\,\)yellow?

Answer: red \(\wedge\, \mathcal{N}\,\)yellow

The red points with a yellow neighbour. The corners of the red frame have none: they touch yellow only diagonally, and on this grid diagonal points are not related.

Surrounded

\(x\) satisfies \(\Phi\,\mathcal{S}\,\Psi\) when \(x\) is in \(\Phi\), and every path from \(x\) that leaves \(\Phi\) passes through \(\Psi\) first.

\( x \in ⟦\Phi\,\mathcal{S}\,\Psi⟧ \iff x \in ⟦\Phi⟧ \;\wedge\; \forall \pi, \ell.\; \big(\pi(0) = x \wedge \pi(\ell) \notin ⟦\Phi⟧\big) \Rightarrow \exists j.\; 0 < j \le \ell \wedge \pi(j) \in ⟦\Psi⟧ \)

  • A path is a sequence of points, each related to the next. In a general closure space, a path is a continuous function from \(\mathbb{N}\).
  • It is a spatial version of the temporal operator until: you are in \(\Phi\), and you cannot get out of \(\Phi\) without stepping on \(\Psi\).

yellow \(\mathcal{S}\) red

Every yellow point satisfies it: the red frame closes the yellow region on all four sides.

Exercise: green \(\mathcal{S}\) violet?

The violet frame has a gap on the right.

Answer: no green point

From every green point there is a path that walks along the green region to the gap and leaves it on a white point. One gap is enough.

Exercise: red \(\mathcal{S}\) white?

No red point. Walking along the frame, every red point reaches a red point next to yellow, and yellow is neither red nor white.

Reachability

\(x\) satisfies \(\rho\,\Phi[\Psi]\) when there is a path from \(x\) to a point of \(\Phi\), whose intermediate points all satisfy \(\Psi\).

\( \Phi\,\mathcal{S}\,\Psi \;\equiv\; \Phi \wedge \neg\, \rho\, \neg(\Phi \vee \Psi)\,[\neg\Psi] \)

Not surrounded: a way out of \(\Phi\) to a point that is neither \(\Phi\) nor \(\Psi\), without meeting \(\Psi\).

Later papers take reachability as the primitive and derive surrounded. On directed graphs there are two reachability operators, one per direction; a distance operator is also added.

Reachability: TACAS 2019. See also Bartocci, Bortolussi, Loreti, Nenzi, MEMOCODE 2017.

Derived operators

\( \Phi \vee \Psi = \neg(\neg\Phi \wedge \neg\Psi) \)or
\( \mathcal{I}\,\Phi = \neg\mathcal{N}\neg\Phi \)interior: the dual of near
\( \mathcal{B}\,\Phi = \mathcal{N}\Phi \wedge \neg\mathcal{I}\Phi \)boundary
\( \mathrm{touch}(\Phi, \Psi) = \Phi \wedge \rho\,(\Phi \wedge \mathcal{N}\Psi)[\Phi] \)the points of \(\Phi\) from which a path inside \(\Phi\) reaches a point near \(\Psi\)
\( \mathrm{grow}(\Phi, \Psi) = \Phi \vee \mathrm{touch}(\Psi, \Phi) \)\(\Phi\), plus the parts of \(\Psi\) that touch it

touch and grow are the words used in the program from lecture 0.

Distance

The Euclidean distance transform gives every pixel its distance from a set, in time linear in the number of pixels. On general graphs, a variant of Dijkstra's algorithm takes \(O(n \log n)\).

C. R. Maurer, R. Qi, V. Raghavan. IEEE TPAMI 25(2), 2003.

Global model checking

For every sub-formula, compute the set of points where it holds, from the atomic propositions up. Each line below is one sub-formula over a graph of nine points.

Each line is a boolean mask; on an image, a black and white image. This is dynamic programming over the syntax of the formula.

Formulas as Python values


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Atom:
    name: str

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Not:
    arg: Formula

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Surrounded:
    left: Formula
    right: Formula

# Near is like Not; And, Or, Touch like Surrounded

type Formula = (Atom | Not | Near | And | Or
                | Surrounded | Touch)

The abstract syntax of SLCS, one class per production, as for the expressions of lecture 4.

An Atom is an atomic proposition: a name such as "blue". Which points satisfy it is not part of the formula; the model says it.

Or and Touch are derived operators. They get a class of their own so that the interpreter can compute them directly.

Parsing a formula


grammar = r"""
    ?formula: bin | mono
    ?mono: atom | unary | paren
    bin: formula OP mono
    unary: UOP mono
    paren: "(" formula ")"
    atom: NAME

    OP: "&" | "|" | "S" | "T"
    UOP: "!" | "N"
    NAME: /[a-z]+/
"""

The same shape as the grammar of lecture 4: binary operators have no precedence and associate to the left.


>>> parse("blue S green")
Surrounded(left=Atom(name='blue'),
           right=Atom(name='green'))
>>> parse("N !green")
Near(arg=Not(arg=Atom(name='green')))

Models


type Point = tuple[int, int]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Model:
    points: frozenset[Point]
    neighbours: dict[Point, frozenset[Point]]
    valuation: dict[str, frozenset[Point]]

def near(a: frozenset[Point], m: Model) -> frozenset[Point]:
    """The closure of a: a, and every point one step away from it."""
    return a | {y for x in a for y in m.neighbours[x]}

The closure model \( (X, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{V}) \) as a Python value: the points, the relation that gives the closure, and the valuation, from names of atomic propositions to sets of points. near is the closure.

A model from an image


def image_model(path: str) -> Model:
    image = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")
    width, height = image.size
    points = frozenset((x, y) for x in range(width)
                              for y in range(height))
    neighbours = {
        (x, y): frozenset(
            (x + dx, y + dy)
            for dx in (-1, 0, 1)
            for dy in (-1, 0, 1)
            if (dx, dy) != (0, 0) and (x + dx, y + dy) in points)
        for (x, y) in points
    }
    valuation = {
        name: frozenset(p for p in points
                        if image.getpixel(p) == rgb)
        for name, rgb in COLOURS.items()
    }
    return Model(points, neighbours, valuation)

The three parts of a closure model, built from a PNG file:

  • the points \(X\): one per pixel;
  • the relation that gives the closure: each pixel and its 8 neighbours;
  • the valuation \(\mathcal{V}\): for each colour name, the pixels of that colour.

A model checker is an interpreter


def evaluate(phi: Formula, m: Model) -> frozenset[Point]:
    match phi:
        case Atom(name):
            return m.valuation[name]
        case Not(arg):
            return m.points - evaluate(arg, m)
        case And(left, right):
            return evaluate(left, m) & evaluate(right, m)
        case Or(left, right):
            return evaluate(left, m) | evaluate(right, m)
        case Near(arg):
            return near(evaluate(arg, m), m)
        case Surrounded(left, right):
            return surrounded(evaluate(left, m),
                              evaluate(right, m), m)
        case Touch(left, right):
            return touch(evaluate(left, m),
                         evaluate(right, m), m)

The same structure as the evaluator of lecture 4.

The values are sets of points instead of numbers. The model plays the role of the environment.

The whole model checker, with a parser for formulas and a reader for PNG images, is code/lesson-11/slcs.py.

Each case, next to its equation

equationcase of evaluate
\( ⟦p⟧ = \mathcal{V}(p) \)Atom(name): the points the valuation gives for that name
\( ⟦\neg\Phi⟧ = X \setminus ⟦\Phi⟧ \)Not(arg): all the points, minus those of the argument
\( ⟦\Phi \wedge \Psi⟧ = ⟦\Phi⟧ \cap ⟦\Psi⟧ \)And: intersection of two Python sets
\( ⟦\Phi \vee \Psi⟧ = ⟦\Phi⟧ \cup ⟦\Psi⟧ \)Or: union
\( ⟦\mathcal{N}\Phi⟧ = \mathcal{C}(⟦\Phi⟧) \)Near: the function near, the closure
\( ⟦\Phi\,\mathcal{S}\,\Psi⟧ \)Surrounded: the function surrounded, next slide
\( ⟦\mathrm{touch}(\Phi, \Psi)⟧ \)Touch: the function touch

Every case first evaluates the sub-formulas, then combines their sets. The recursion follows the syntax, as in lecture 4.

Surrounded: flooding from the outside


def surrounded(a, b, m):
    good = set(a)
    leaks = {y for x in a
               for y in m.neighbours[x]} - a - b
    while leaks:
        lost = {x for y in leaks
                  for x in m.neighbours[y]} & good
        good -= lost
        leaks = lost - b
    return frozenset(good)

The definition speaks about all paths. The algorithm does not enumerate them.

  • A leak is a point next to a that is in neither a nor b.
  • A point of a next to a leak is lost.
  • A lost point that is not in b is a leak in its turn.

Every point is lost at most once, so the time is linear in the size of the graph.

Flooding green \(\mathcal{S}\) violet

The leak: the white point in the gap of the violet frame, next to green (ringed).

Step 1. The green points next to a leak are lost (crossed); the points lost at this step are the next leaks (ringed).

Step 2. The green points next to a leak are lost (crossed); the points lost at this step are the next leaks (ringed).

Step 3. The green points next to a leak are lost (crossed); the points lost at this step are the next leaks (ringed).

Step 4. The green points next to a leak are lost (crossed); the points lost at this step are the next leaks (ringed).

Step 5. The green points next to a leak are lost (crossed); the points lost at this step are the next leaks (ringed).

No leaks are left, and every green point is lost: green S violet holds nowhere.

Touch: a visit from the target


def touch(a, b, m):
    reached = set(a & near(b, m))
    frontier = set(reached)
    while frontier:
        frontier = {y for x in frontier
                      for y in m.neighbours[x]} & a - reached
        reached |= frontier
    return frozenset(reached)

Start from the points of a that are near b, and visit a from there, breadth first. Each point is visited once.

When the relation is symmetric, as on images, the same set can be computed with connected components: the components of a that contain a point near b. This is how the GPU version of VoxLogicA does it.

How much it costs

¬ ∧ ∨one pass over the points
nearone pass over the points and their neighbours
surroundedflooding: each point is lost at most once
touch, reacha visit, or connected components
distancelinear on images; \(O(n \log n)\) on graphs

A formula is computed with one such pass per sub-formula, and each sub-formula is computed once.

Checking formulas on an image

A small image with four colours. Three green islands: one with a blue lake inside, one next to a blue pool, one alone. A black item touches the pool.

On the next slides each formula is checked with slcs.py. The points where it holds are in orange.


$ python3 slcs.py

Atoms, near, interior

The interior is the dual of near: the points of green whose neighbours are all green.

Surrounded and touch

The lake is surrounded by green; the pool is not, it touches white. The last formula: the green islands touching a blue region that touches black.

VoxLogicA

A spatial model checker for images, in 2D and 3D.

  • Written in F#, on .NET.
  • Image operations from ITK, the Insight Toolkit, through SimpleITK.
  • Reads PNG, BMP, NIfTI and the other formats ITK reads.

Its predecessor, topochecker, was written in OCaml and checked SLCS and its spatio-temporal extension on graphs.

VoxLogicA was presented at TACAS 2019 together with its language, ImgQL.

The key idea: never compute the same thing twice. Identical sub-expressions are computed once.

G. Belmonte, V. Ciancia, D. Latella, M. Massink. VoxLogicA: A Spatial Model Checker for Declarative Image Analysis. TACAS, LNCS 11427, 2019.

ImgQL

  • The logical core: SLCS, with reachability and distance.
  • Colours and thresholds, normalisation.
  • Imaging primitives and texture analysis.
  • Global values: volume, maximum, minimum.
  • Functions, defined with let. No recursion.

load base = "exercise.png"

let b = (red(base) =. 0) & (green(base) =. 0)
        & (blue(base) =. 255)
let g = (red(base) =. 0) & (green(base) =. 255)
        & (blue(base) =. 0)

save "near-blue.png" N b
save "blue-S-green.png" b S g
save "green-T-blue.png" g T b

The operators with a dot work point by point: red(base) =. 0 is true at the pixels whose red component is 0. Full program: code/lesson-11/exercise.imgql.

The library is written in ImgQL


let !(a) = not(a)
let N(a) = near(a)
let I(a) = interior(a)
let ~>(a,b) = through(b,a)
let mayReach(a,b) = N((b ~> N a) | a) // This is the \rho operator from TACAS19
let touch(a,b) = a ~> N b
let grow(a,b) = (a | touch(b,a))
let surrounded(a,b) = a \ mayReach(not(a | b),not(b))
let T(a,b) = touch(a,b)
let S(a,b) = surrounded(a,b)

From stdlib.imgql, the library of VoxLogicA 1: the derived operators of the logic, defined as ImgQL functions on top of a few primitives (near, interior, through).

A complete program: the maze


load base = "maze.png"

let isColor(img, rc, gc, bc) =
  (red(img) =. rc) & (green(img) =. gc)
  & (blue(img) =. bc)

let g = isColor(base, 0, 255, 0)
let b = isColor(base, 0, 0, 255)
let w = isColor(base, 255, 255, 255)

let pathToExit = w T g
let pathFromItem = w T b

save "maze-1.png" overlay(pathToExit)
save "maze-5.png" overlay(b T pathToExit)

The maze: results

The corridors that lead to the exit; those that lead to an item but not to the exit; those that lead to neither; the items that can escape. No search algorithm was written in the program.

Running it


$ VoxLogicA maze.imgql

The program and the image are in code/lesson-11/. The outputs maze-1.png … maze-5.png are written next to the program.

Try changing the program: which corridors are reachable from the item in the middle? Which items cannot reach each other?

Values are whole images

For a model checker, the value of an expression is the set of points where it holds. For an image, that is another image.

A brain scan has about nine million voxels. Every intermediate value of a program is an image of that size, and computing one costs time and memory.

The first design rule of the interpreter: never compute anything twice.

Maximal sharing

The expression i(f(g(x), h(g(x))), h(g(x))) contains g(x) three times and h(g(x)) twice.

A table of sub-expressions


ids = {}

def node(op, *args):
    key = (op, args)
    if key not in ids:
        ids[key] = len(ids)
    return ids[key]

The parser does not build a tree. For each sub-expression it calls node with the operator and the numbers of the arguments, built before.

ids gives each pair (op, args) a number. A new pair gets the next free one: with len(ids) entries, the numbers used so far are 0 … len(ids) - 1. A pair seen before gets its old number back.

Building the example

The calls for i(f(g(x), h(g(x))), h(g(x))), in the order the parser makes them:

callresult
node("x")new: 0
node("g", 0)new: 1
node("x")found: 0
node("g", 0)found: 1
node("h", 1)new: 2
callresult
node("f", 1, 2)new: 3
node("x")found: 0
node("g", 0)found: 1
node("h", 1)found: 2
node("i", 3, 2)new: 4

Ten calls, one per node of the syntax tree. Five entries in the table: the five nodes of the graph with maximal sharing.

Evaluating the table


values = {}
for (op, args), i in ids.items():
    values[i] = OPS[op](*(values[a] for a in args))

The arguments of a node always have smaller numbers than the node: they were built first. So the table can be evaluated in the order of its numbers, and every argument is ready when it is needed.

For a formula, this is the global model checking algorithm: one set of points per sub-formula, from the atoms up.

A program denotes a graph


let a = N blue
let onGreen = a & green
let onWhite = a & white
save "out.png" onGreen | onWhite

Each node is an operation; its arguments are the nodes below it. The small number is the node's identifier in the table.

A let gives a name to a node. The names are not in the graph: a is the node N, which has two parents and is computed once.

The same graph, without let


save "out.png" (N blue & green) | (N blue & white)

N blue is written twice, and the table gives it the same number twice. The graph is the one of the previous slide.

Sharing does not depend on let: it is found from the syntax. A let is there for the reader.

Functions are expanded


let grow(a, b) = a | touch(b, a)

save "out.png" grow(red, yellow) | grow(red, green)

A call is replaced by the body of the function, with the arguments in place of the parameters. With no recursion, the expansion always ends.

After the expansion, red occurs four times in the text and once in the graph.

The value of each node

(N blue & green) | (N blue & white) on the exercise image: each node holds a set of points, computed once from the nodes below it.

What was left out

ImgQL has let and functions, and no recursion, no loops, no conditionals on data.

  1. Every function call can be expanded before running, so every program terminates.
  2. The whole computation is a graph before it starts.
  3. Independent nodes of the graph can run in parallel, with no annotation in the source.

Leaving out recursion was a design decision, and these three properties of the implementation follow from it.

Parallel, and on the GPU

On the CPU

The nodes of the graph are tasks. VoxLogicA runs them on all the cores, with dynamic scheduling (the F# library Hopac). Each task is an operation on a whole image, so the overhead of scheduling is small.

On the GPU

VoxLogicA-GPU is a massively parallel implementation. Reachability is computed with connected components, which have good parallel algorithms.

L. Bussi, V. Ciancia, F. Gadducci. FORTE 2021.

The interface

Back to the tumour

Glioblastoma, on a FLAIR scan: the tumour and the swelling around it are brighter than healthy tissue.

The procedure has three steps. Each is a few lines of ImgQL, and each line can be read aloud.

Step 1: remove the background


let background = touch(intensity <. 0.1, border)
let brain = !background

The background is the dark area that touches the border of the image. The brain is the rest.

A plain threshold would also remove the dark areas inside the brain. touch keeps them.

Step 2: thresholds on percentiles


let pflair = percentiles(intensity, brain, 0.5)
let hyperIntense = flt(5.0, pflair >. 0.95)
let veryIntense = flt(2.0, pflair >. 0.86)

Percentiles make the thresholds relative to the intensities of each brain. flt removes the parts narrower than a ball of the given radius. Hyper-intense areas are tumour; very intense areas sometimes are.

Step 3: grow, then texture


let growTum = grow(hyperIntense, veryIntense)
let tumSim = similarTo(growTum)
let tumStatCC = flt(2.0, tumSim >. 0.6)
let gtv = grow(growTum, tumStatCC)

Keep the very intense areas only where they touch a hyper-intense one. Then grow once more into the regions whose texture is similar to the tumour.

The texture similarity is a statistical operator, not a logical one.

Results

210
high-grade gliomas of BraTS 2017, with accuracy in line with the state of the art
5–10s
per 3D image, about nine million voxels, on a desktop
~12
lines of ImgQL for the whole procedure

Other images, other spaces

Also: bike sharing and buses in space and time, with the logic STLCS (ISoLA 2016, STTT 2018); video streams (DataMod 2021); 3D meshes, with PolyLogicA (AiML 2024).

How accurate is accurate?

The usual score is the Dice–Sørensen coefficient between the computed region \(X\) and the reference \(Y\):

\( \mathrm{Dice}(X, Y) = \dfrac{2\,|X \cap Y|}{|X| + |Y|} \)

\(|X|\) is the volume of \(X\): its number of voxels. 1 is a perfect overlap, 0 is no overlap. Eighteen methods of the BraTS 2017 challenge scored 0.88 on average, from 0.64 to 0.96.

In BraTS the reference is drawn by up to four human raters and merged by a voting rule.

A score of 0.97 means that the method reproduces how a few people drew a boundary, as merged by a rule. Different experts draw different boundaries.

The Dice coefficient, in a picture

Blue: the reference only. Orange: the computed region only. Violet: both. Dice is twice the violet area, divided by the orange area plus the blue area, each counted with the violet.

Left: a small error on the boundary. Centre: the same shape, shifted. Right: the right place, but too small.

Dice does not see where the error is

On the right the region is exact, plus a small false region far away. It has the higher Dice: the extra region is a few pixels. For radiotherapy it is a dose in the wrong place.

Metrics, revisited

Unsuitable algorithms could be wrongly regarded as the best-performing ones.

A. Reinke, …, L. Maier-Hein. Understanding metric-related pitfalls in image analysis validation. Nature Methods 21, 2024.

With a readable procedure one can ask what a score measures: which part of the boundary, which rule of the rater. A score alone does not say.

HD95: how far the boundaries are

For each boundary point of one region, take the distance to the nearest boundary point of the other. The Hausdorff distance is the largest of these distances.

HD95 is the 95th percentile instead of the largest: the worst 5% of the points are ignored, so one stray pixel does not decide the score. On scans it is measured in millimetres; lower is better.

The computed boundary, coloured by its distance from the reference boundary: blue within 3 pixels, orange farther. The large region coincides with the reference.

NSD: a Dice for boundaries

\( \mathrm{NSD}_\tau = \dfrac{|\partial X \cap B_\tau(\partial Y)| + |\partial Y \cap B_\tau(\partial X)|}{|\partial X| + |\partial Y|} \)

The boundary points of each region within a tolerance \(\tau\) of the other boundary (blue), out of all boundary points. Here \(\tau = 1.5\) pixels. It says how much of the contour would need correcting.

Logic and neural networks

A procedure in the logic

  • Can be read, discussed, checked against guidelines.
  • Needs no training data: a new idea can be tried at once.
  • Does not learn from examples, and does not generalise by itself.

A neural network

  • Learns from annotated examples.
  • nnU-Net configures itself on a new dataset; it is a standard reference for segmentation.
  • Cannot be read: its rule is in its weights.

F. Isensee, P. F. Jaeger, S. A. A. Kohl, J. Petersen, K. H. Maier-Hein. nnU-Net. Nature Methods 18, 2021.

Training and prediction as primitives


let tumour_dataset_augmented =
    ground_truth_dataset + apply_threshold(tumour_threshold, ground_truth_dataset)

let tumour_model = train(tumour_dataset_augmented)
let oedema_model = train(oedema_dataset_augmented)

let ML_tumour_core = predict(tumour_model, validation_dataset)
let ML_oedema = predict(oedema_model, validation_dataset)

let oedema = touch(ML_oedema, ML_tumour_core)

The output of the oedema network is noisy. The last line is a logical rule: keep the oedema that touches the tumour core found by the other network.

From the presentation of VoxLogicA 2 at ISoLA 2024, LNCS 15222.

The dataset is the value


result = for path in paths do
    let img = ReadImage(path) in
    let mm = MinimumMaximum(img) in
    let lo = index(mm, 0) in
    let hi = index(mm, 1) in
    let thresholds = lo + (hi - lo) * (idxs / 99) in
    for th in thresholds do
        volume(BinaryThreshold(img, th, hi, 255, 0))

In VoxLogicA 2 a value can be a whole dataset, and for builds new datasets from it. A sweep over many images and many thresholds is one expression.

Adapted from the gallery of VoxLogicA 2. Every SimpleITK filter is available under its own name.

A program is a graph of tasks

Maximal sharing, one level up: the nodes are now training runs, predictions and whole datasets.

The graph is evaluated lazily, its results are stored, and independent tasks run in parallel.

Different nodes can run in different places, close to the data: a hospital need not send its images away.

Is the computation deterministic?

A cache keyed on the syntax assumes that the same expression always has the same value.

touch(a, b), percentiles(img, mask, 0.5): same arguments, same result. Storing it is safe.

train(dataset): two runs give two different networks. Which one is "the value"? The one computed first, the one computed here, or train(model, date, place)?

This is a question about the semantics of the language, and the design of the cache depends on its answer.

What the two can do for each other

Logic checks networks

Where guidelines are published, a specification can check whether the output of a network respects them.

Networks inform logic

Fit the thresholds of a specification to the output of a network: the fitted procedure says, in readable terms, a rule the network is following.

G. Belmonte, V. Ciancia, M. Imbriani. Two Hybrid-AI Case Studies for VoxLogicA 2. AISoLA 2025, to appear.

Symbolic and hybrid AI, AIIM 2025

Two contributions, on BraTS 2017, 2019 and 2020:

  • the symbolic procedure of TACAS 2019, extended and evaluated;
  • a hybrid method: nnU-Net is used to choose the numeric parameters of the ImgQL procedure, image by image.

The mask is computed by the logic; the network only helps choose two numbers.

G. Belmonte, V. Ciancia, M. Massink. Symbolic and hybrid AI for brain tissue segmentation using spatial model checking. Artificial Intelligence in Medicine 167, 103154, 2025. Open access.

Two numbers decide the procedure


let hyperIntense = flt(5.0, pflair >. hI)
let veryIntense  = flt(2.0, pflair >. vI)
let tumour = grow(hyperIntense, veryIntense)

hI and vI are percentile thresholds. On the 293 high-grade cases of BraTS 2020, the best single pair for all images is hI = 0.93, vI = 0.88, with mean Dice 0.826.

vI matters much more than hI: the three curves almost coincide.

One pair for all, or one pair per image?

For each image, try every pair (hI, vI) of the grid and keep the one with the best Dice against the reference.

On 234 cases the mean Dice goes from 0.848 with one fixed pair to 0.884 with the best pair for each image. On one image it goes from 0.66 to 0.86.

So the language can express a much better segmentation of each image: the procedure is right, the numbers are not.

But choosing the pair needs the reference, which a new image does not have. This is not yet a method.

The method: nnU-Net in place of the answer

nnU-Net is trained once, on 50 annotated cases. For a new image its mask takes the place of the reference: the thresholds are chosen so that the ImgQL mask agrees with it as much as possible.

If the best agreement is low, the two methods disagree on that image, and an expert should look at it.

Results on 234 cases

methodmean Dice (sd)median
fixed thresholds0.85 (0.11)0.88
thresholds chosen with nnU-Net0.87 (0.09)0.90
best thresholds, knowing the answer0.88 (0.08)0.91
nnU-Net alone0.89 (0.08)0.91

Choosing the thresholds with the network raises the mean Dice by about 0.02 and lowers the spread; the difference from fixed thresholds is significant (Wilcoxon, p < 0.01). The result is an ImgQL procedure with two numbers that an expert can read and change.

The 234 cases exclude the 50 used to train nnU-Net. Table 6 of the paper.

One case, five segmentations

A case chosen in the paper because the methods differ most. Green: the reference. With fixed thresholds the region is too large; with thresholds chosen by agreement with nnU-Net it shrinks towards the reference. Dice against the reference is under each image.

BraTS 2020, case 099. From the paper, Fig. 9 (axial view).

VoxLogicA 2.1: same language, new engine

What stays

  • The language: programs accepted by 2.0 run with the same meaning and give the same values.
  • Every primitive, nnU-Net training and prediction included.
  • The library of VoxLogicA 1, as the namespace vox1.

What changes

  • The scheduler, the workers and the store are written in Rust.
  • The image operations stay in Python, on free-threaded Python, so they run on many threads at once.
  • The part of the scheduler that decides what runs next is generated from a formal model.

Status: release candidate; a pre-release was tagged on 12 November 2026.

Why model the scheduler

The scheduler decides, at every event, which node to create, which primitive to start, what to keep in memory, when a goal is delivered. Many things happen at once.

The bugs of such code depend on the order of events: a deadlock, a goal never delivered, a value dropped while someone still needs it.

A test runs one order of events. A model checker explores all of them, on a model of the scheduler.

In VoxLogicA 2.1 the deciding part of the scheduler is written as a model first, checked, and then turned into code automatically.

mCRL2


act dispatch, done: Nat;

proc Core(running: Nat) =
    (running < 2) -> dispatch(running) . Core(running + 1)
  + (running > 0) -> done(running) . Core(Int2Nat(running - 1));

init Core(0);

A process algebra with data. The code:

  • act: two actions. Core(running): a process whose state is how many jobs run.
  • c -> a . P: if c holds, do a, then behave as P. If fewer than 2 run, start one; if any runs, one finishes.
  • +: either step, whichever is enabled. init: start with none running.

The state space of this process: at most two jobs running. A toy example, not the engine's model.

J. F. Groote, M. R. Mousavi. Modeling and Analysis of Communicating Systems. MIT Press, 2014. O. Bunte et al. The mCRL2 Toolset for Analysing Concurrent Systems. TACAS 2019.

Properties: modal logic again

Properties are formulas of the modal μ-calculus, read on the state space as on a Kripke frame. \([a]\Phi\) is the box: after every \(a\), \(\Phi\). \(\langle a\rangle\Phi\) is the diamond: some \(a\), then \(\Phi\).

[(!finish)*] <true> trueno deadlock: until the run finishes, after any sequence of steps, some step is possible
mu X . ([!finish] X && <true> true)every run ends: \(\mu\) is a least fixed point, so on every path finish comes eventually
[true* . misorder] falseprogram order: no sequence of steps ends in a goal delivered out of order

Three of the 28 properties of the engine's model, as written in the repository. D. Kozen. Results on the propositional μ-calculus. Theoretical Computer Science 27, 1983.

Minimisation

Two states are bisimilar when each can do every step the other can, to states that are again bisimilar. Merging bisimilar states gives a smaller system that satisfies the same μ-calculus formulas. mCRL2 does it with ltsconvert, and compares two systems with ltscompare.

The same idea works for space: MiniLogicA minimises an image, seen as a closure model, up to spatial bisimilarity.

From model to code

Each step of the model is condition -> action . Core(new values); an action is an event from outside or a decision of the scheduler. naima-codegen writes the same machine in Rust and in Python.

Model + policy: what really happens

  • The problem. In the model, several decisions can be enabled at once, and mCRL2 explores them all. Code must take one.
  • The policy. A fixed priority among the decisions, plus a rule for which item: finish started work first, free memory before starting new work, then the oldest loop element.
  • The refined system is the model with the policy written into it: at every state, one decision. All the properties are checked again on it. On small models the tool also checks trace inclusion: every run of the refined system is a run of the model. VoxLogicA's full model is too large for that check.

Rust and Python together

The engine is a Rust library loaded into Python. The image operations stay in Python and its libraries. Python 3.14 can run without the global interpreter lock, so several primitives run at the same time on different threads.

Limits of the guarantee

  • The properties are checked on a set of reference programs, with loops over up to 8 cases nested up to 4 deep. Deeper programs are tested, not proved.
  • They cover the deciding part. A primitive that never returns, or a library that crashes, is outside the model; the engine watches for those while it runs.
  • The bound counts evaluations, not bytes. Memory is handled by reading it while the program runs.

NAIMA, a project tracker for AI agents

  • The agents do the work and ask; the owner answers. Each answer is recorded as a decision, with its reason.
  • Requirements, bugs, tests and decisions are items in the repository itself.
  • An item is closed only with a passed test and the commit that lands it.
  • Optionally, the critical parts are modelled and checked with mCRL2.

Free and open source: naima-project.github.io. First commit 29 September 2026; version 1.0 on 1 October, 1.1 on 30 October.

Lines of work

The coordinator works on the main line and is the only one who lands changes on it. Each worker agent works on a line of its own; a goal or a release is a station that holds when its tests pass.

Measured on every commit

Tests, coverage, lines of code, open bugs, function size: recorded at each commit, with their history. The screens show NAIMA's own project (final design of the new interface, November 2026).

How 2.1 was built

  • On 5 October 2026 the plan of the reimplementation was written in the tracker: the owner's decisions, the phases, the work items and their dependencies.
  • Each milestone is a gate that holds when a runnable test proves it.
  • The person states the invariants: memory stays bounded, every node goes through one code path, the scheduler is generated from the model. The agents write the code.

Anthropic's AI for Science program

An award of Claude usage credits, given in September 2026 for one project: brain-tumour segmentation in which Claude writes the procedures in VoxLogicA's spatial logic.

  • The result is a mask together with a program that explains it, not the output of a network.
  • This needed a perfectly stable VoxLogicA: the agent runs thousands of programs unattended, and one crash or one wrong value spoils the experiment. Writing that engine needed the model checker of the previous slides.

The work is not published yet; the latest numbers, preliminary, are at the end of the lecture.

How the loop runs

Who does what

The person

Direction and invariants: what must never happen, which failure matters, when a number is suspicious, what the guidelines and the anatomy require.

The agent

Mechanism and measurement: writes the programs in the language, runs them, tabulates, renders the images, proposes the next step.

The agent does not write arbitrary code into the result. It writes expressions in a small language whose primitives a person chose, and whose output a person can look at.

A language a person can read

A trained network

A few of its weights. Its rule is in millions of numbers like these; changing an idea means training again.

A procedure in the language

!touch(flair <. 0.1, border)what is not dark and connected to the border
pflair >. 0.95the brightest 5% of the brain
grow(hyperIntense, veryIntense)the brightest parts, extended into the bright parts touching them

Each line can be read aloud, discussed with a radiologist, and changed in a few seconds; the engine recomputes only what changed.

Why the language makes the loop possible

Without a language

An idea costs a training run: hours of computation, a new model, and a result that cannot be read.

With a language

An idea costs a few lines: add an operator, run again, look at the images. The person can check every step the agent proposes, because it is written in words of the domain.

A parameter sweep is itself a program in the language, so a whole experiment can be stored, shared and resumed like any other program.

Where the experiment stands, November 2026

  • The procedure: 23 candidate formulas, 195 lines of ImgQL, no training.
  • For each image, the formula and its thresholds are chosen by agreement with the mask of nnU-Net, found by a bisection search over the thresholds.
  • The oracle, choosing with the reference in hand, measures what the 23 formulas can express.
60 cases100 cases
procedure0.900.90
oracle0.92
nnU-Net0.930.93

Mean Dice. 60 validation cases of BraTS 2020 never seen by nnU-Net; 100 held-out cases of BraTS 2023. Preliminary and unpublished.

Conclusions: semantics and logic

  • We started from a semantic domain, closure spaces, then wrote a logic on it, then an interpreter for the logic. The order was the same as for the calculator of lecture 4.
  • A formula denotes a set of points. A model checker computes that set: it is an evaluator, and maximal sharing turns it into dynamic programming.
  • The same modal operators, box and diamond, appeared three times: on topological spaces, on images, and on the state space of the scheduler.

Conclusions: verification

  • Model checking was used twice: as the interpreter of the spatial logic, and to verify the scheduler that runs it.
  • The deciding part of the scheduler is generated from the verified model, and the generated code is checked against it again.
  • Future work: proving with Lean, an interactive theorem prover, that the engine as a whole respects the properties, beyond the reference programs.

L. de Moura, S. Ullrich. The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language. CADE 2021.

Conclusions: vision, networks and language models

The person states intentions and invariants; a language model writes procedures in the domain-specific language; the engine runs them, with neural networks trained and used inside the same program; the person reads the procedure and the images. The result: masks at about 0.90 Dice, each explained by a readable procedure.

What to take home

  1. Decide what a program means before choosing its syntax. Here a formula means a set of points in a closure space.
  2. Keep the core small: six constructs. grow, touch and distance are not built in; they are a library written in the language.
  3. No recursion, no unbounded loops: every program terminates, nothing is computed twice, independent parts run in parallel.
  4. Name the primitives after the domain. A radiologist can read grow(hyperIntense, veryIntense); nobody can read the weights of a network.
  5. When the result is wrong, the program shows where. A score only says by how much.
